title: Repertoire at the Villa: Dixieland, Charleston and blues
summary: They played Dixieland, the Charleston craze, and blues in a modern way.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: What kind of pieces did you play at the villa with Fess and Joe Howard? Was it sort of jazz band, or was it more just straight marches or waltzes? What kind of members did you play?

Oh no, no, we played real Dixieland. Dixieland style. Yeah, style, you know. And when I was there with Gabriel, the dance came out to call, what do you call that dance again? They go fast, you know, just faster you play the-
Was it Charleston? Was that the Charleston?

Yeah, the Charleston. And that would ruin the wives and the husband. They used to give dances, you know, the private dances. And women just went wild over that dance, and they just thought they could do anything, you know, and that kind of, you know, broke up couples that would have been together maybe the day, but for that dance. Just like the teenagers now smoking and going home. See, with all that just a temptation to nothing, you might as well say, in the long run. The fellas getting up there singing the blues, saying everything, and they're out there dancing, doing everything. Well, it's kind of a disgrace now, with the music that they produce now, you know.
I was going to ask about the blues, if you ever played in the district, did you ever play blues there at the villa?
Yeah, we played blues, but played in a modern way, you know. They didn't, you know. Now, I'll tell you what, they're playing the blues in churches now in a way.
